name: Ivan Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Becker brothers at Oakfield, a pig farm with about three thousand pigs being grown on for meat, plus maize and barley we grow for their feed. I start at six, walk the pens, check the feeders and water nipples, and pull out any pig that's off its food. Afternoons I'm on the tractor or in the feed mill. I've been there two years and I'm still learning the pigs, they're cleverer than people think.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before Oakfield?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty years as a maintenance fitter at the sugar beet factory on the edge of town, keeping the conveyors and pumps running. The owners shut it and moved production abroad, and I got a decent payout. Marta, my wife, said don't sit at home, you'll drive me mad. So the Beckers took me on, mainly because I can fix the feed system when it jams, which it does twice a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you are, a lot of noise and not much in it. I'd say it to the Beckers over coffee in the office. They're practical men, they'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good. I've got maybe seven years left, and I want to spend them getting good at the pigs and keeping the feed mill going. I don't need a revolution, I've had one already when the factory shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep using the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to find part numbers and the manual for some pump nobody's made since 1998, because it's quicker than ringing round. Money stays as it is, we're comfortable, the house is paid off and the factory payout is in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Satisfied, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you give me an example of using it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the feed auger, that's the big screw that moves feed along a pipe, kept stopping. I photographed the motor plate and asked the phone what the fault might be, and it gave me three ideas. The second one was right. That's useful, but it's a tool, like a good spanner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Tomasz is doing an apprenticeship as an electrician. I'd tell him to get his tickets and work hard, same as always. A trade is a trade.

S0.say: I'd say there you are, a lot of noise and not much in it, to the owners over coffee in the office. They're practical men and would agree.
S0.think: It's good for me: I've maybe seven years left to get good at the pigs and keep the feed mill going. I've already had one upheaval when the factory shut.
S0.do: Carries on as he is, using phone AI now and then to find part numbers and old pump manuals. Keeps money as it is, with a paid-off house and his factory payout in the bank, and tells his apprentice son to keep working for his tickets.
S0.quote: That's useful, but it's a tool, like a good spanner.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is a practical fitter who sees AI as one more tool in the box. His previous job went abroad, not to machines, which shapes where he puts the blame. He values trades and apprenticeships, as his son's path shows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines need fixing, and somebody's got to do it. I'd say it to the lads at the farm and at the social club. And I'd say the answer is apprenticeships and hard work, not the government paying people to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in a decent spot. I'm junior on the pigs, but I'm the one who keeps the machines running, and more machines means more breakdowns. I'm not frightened of this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen what the other farms were buying, I'd ask the Beckers to send me on the course for the robot feeders and the automatic pen cleaners, so I'm the man who fixes them. I'd use the AI tools a bit more for fault-finding. I'd keep our money as it is, maybe put a bit toward Tomasz's van when he finishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit interested, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Oakfield would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Kasia, she does the pens and the piglet work and she's very good with animals, but she's not mechanical. I'd tell the Beckers, keep her, the robots won't spot a sick pig like she does. Whether they listen is up to them, it's their farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you blame the Beckers if they cut jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's their right. They've put their own money in, they take the risk. But I'd tell them straight if I thought they were making a mistake, I'm not shy.

S1.say: I'd say machines need fixing and somebody has to do it. The answer is apprenticeships and hard work, not government paying people to sit at home.
S1.think: I'm in a decent spot: junior on the pigs, but the one who keeps the machines running, and more machines means more breakdowns.
S1.do: Waits to see what other farms buy, then asks the owners to send him on courses for robot feeders and pen cleaners. Uses AI tools more for fault-finding and may help his son buy a van.
S1.quote: I'd tell the Beckers, keep her, the robots won't spot a sick pig like she does.
S1.fieldNote: He sees himself as the person who fixes the new machines, which makes this picture an opportunity. He defends the owners' right to decide but would speak up for a colleague. His view of public help is that work and training beat handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is far too fast, and the men who build these things should be made to slow down. I don't like governments meddling, but this is like a factory with no safety rules. I'd say it at the club, and loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if robots can fix robots, then I've got nothing. My job at Oakfield is gone by 60. I'd be fine for money, but I'd feel useless, and I've never been useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd make sure our savings are safe and spread out, and I'd buy the field behind our house that old Mrs Weber is selling, about four hectares. Land doesn't disappear. Once it hit, I'd keep a few pigs and hens on that land and grow our own, and help Tomasz however I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for the house, for my sense of myself, and for Tomasz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years of warning. What does that short window take away from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. With ten years I'd be retired and watching. With two, I'm thrown out at 60 and Tomasz finishes his apprenticeship into a world where a robot wires the houses. He'd have done everything right and still be stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the work dried up, who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta's family. Her brother's got a building firm and he's said Tomasz can always work there. If that goes too, we'd all have to pull together, the family, the church. That's how my parents got through hard times.

S2.say: I'd say this is far too fast and the people building these things should be made to slow down. I don't like governments meddling, but this is like a factory with no safety rules.
S2.think: If robots can fix robots, I've got nothing, and my job is gone by 60. I'd be fine for money but I'd feel useless, and I've never been useless.
S2.do: Makes sure savings are safe and spread out, and buys a four-hectare field behind the house. Once AGI arrives, keeps pigs and hens and grows food on it, and leans on family and church while helping his son.
S2.feel: Anxious, not for the house but for his sense of himself and for his son.
S2.fieldNote: Even as a free-market man he calls for rules in this picture, comparing it to a factory without safety rules. The two-year window hits his son hardest, who'd have done everything right. His answer is land, family and church rather than state help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so get your trade, get your land, and look after your own. I'd say the government should set fair rules but not try to run everything. And I'd tell the young ones to learn to fix the new machines while there's still a need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be 63, which isn't far off when I'd planned to stop. It's Tomasz I'd think about. Five years gives him time to move into something where he's still needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the robot maintenance course in the first year, so I'm useful at Oakfield for as long as possible. I'd buy Mrs Weber's field over the next couple of years, not in a rush. And I'd sit down with Tomasz and talk about adding robot servicing or solar work to his electrical tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But I'd feel like I had my hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the robots. Do you mean that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Once the first few farms had them, and I'd seen them running, I'd want to learn them properly. Same as I did with the computer controls at the factory in the nineties. I wasn't first, but I wasn't last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would faith come into this for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pray for help, but I'd not wait for it. My father always said God helps those who get up early.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years, so get your trade, get your land and look after your own. Government should set fair rules but not try to run everything.
S3.think: I'd be 63, not far off when I'd planned to stop. Five years gives my son time to move into something where he's still needed.
S3.do: Takes a robot maintenance course in the first year to stay useful at the farm and buys the field behind his house over a couple of years. Talks with his son about adding robot servicing or solar work to his electrical qualifications.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with his hands on the wheel.
S3.quote: My father always said God helps those who get up early.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets his steady style work: wait for proof, then learn properly, as he did with factory controls. Land, family and trades remain his anchors. Faith is a spur to act, not a reason to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and anyone who can't get ready in ten years isn't trying. I'd say it, but kindly. People do need help sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be retired, 68, with a field and some pigs, I hope. I'm not too worried for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Oakfield, learn the new machines when they're proven, retire at 65. Buy the field when it's right. Keep nudging Tomasz to keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Mostly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz over those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to him, be like a good fitter. Learn the new machine before it arrives. Don't wait for the manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn things once they're proven. Is there a risk in waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd be too soft on myself. I've said I'll learn when it's proven, but by the time it's proven, maybe all the jobs are taken. That's a fair point, I'll think about it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time, and anyone who can't get ready in ten years isn't trying. I'd say it kindly, because people do need help sometimes.
S4.think: I'd be retired at 68 with a field and some pigs, I hope. I'm not too worried for myself.
S4.do: Carries on at the farm, learns new machines once proven and retires at 65. Buys the field when the time is right and keeps nudging his son to keep learning.
S4.quote: Learn the new machine before it arrives. Don't wait for the manual.
S4.fieldNote: When asked about the risk of waiting for proof, he takes the point and admits it. His advice to his son contradicts his own wait-and-see habit, which he notices. The long window leaves him personally calm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd lose my use, and Tomasz would lose his trade before he'd even started. What would help is rules that slow it down a bit, and money going into apprenticeships and helping families stand on their own feet, not just a cheque in the post.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You might ask what makes a man feel useful. For me it was always being the one they shout for when the line stops. If nobody shouts for you any more, money doesn't fix that.

headlineQuote: If nobody shouts for you any more, money doesn't fix that.
portrait: Ivan Kowalski is 58 and was a maintenance fitter at a sugar beet factory for thirty years until it moved abroad; now he's a junior hand on the Becker brothers' pig farm, kept on partly because he can fix the feed system. He uses AI now and then like a good spanner and learns new machines once he's seen them work. Financially comfortable with a paid-off house, he sees the milder pictures as a chance to be the man who fixes the robots. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious about feeling useless and about his son, an apprentice electrician. He answers with land, family, church and trades, and even as a free-market man wants rules to slow things down.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he'd lose his usefulness and his son would lose his trade before it started.
whatWouldHelp: Rules to slow the change down, and money for apprenticeships and helping families stand on their own feet rather than handouts.
